newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Daiwa Bank manager gets 2 months prison.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Daiwa Bank manager gets 2 months prison.

text.p: A federal judge Friday sentenced the former general manager of the New York branch of Daiwa Bank Ltd to two months in prison for helping to conceal $1.1 billion in trading losses at the bank from Federal authorities.
Masahiro Tsuda, 54, was also fined $100,000, sentenced to one year of probation, and must post a $50,000 security bond.
Tsuda had pleaded guilty to the charge in April before U.S. District Judge Sidney H. Stein. The plea agreement provided that prosecutors drop a count of concealing a felony.

In February, Daiwa Bank pleaded guilty to charges of concealing the loss and agreed to pay $340 million in fines, the largest criminal fine levied against a financial institution in the United States.

The charges stem from the conduct of its top management during the summer of 1995 when managers deliberately covered up huge trading losses incurred by Toshihide Iguschi, an executive vice president at the New York branch.
Iguchi pleaded guilty to charges of doctoring bank records and embezzlement, stemming from the $1.1 billion in trading losses that he accumulated and covered up over 12 years.

Tsuda said that although he had violated American laws, he had done so at the behest of his superiors at Daiwa, which is based in Osaka, Japan, and of Japan's Ministry of Finance. He said he had taken similar actions in the late 1980's to cover up a $30 million trading loss.

Although the probation department had recommended that Tsuda receive no prison sentence, Judge Stein said he was imposing the two-month term because the defendant had been a manager and directed others to help in the scheme. He said the prison term would also deter foreign corporations and their employees from breaking U.S. laws.
Stein said that if he did not give Tsuda a prison term it would encourage foreign defendants to violate the law with the risk of only minimal penalities.
"A message must be sent ...United States laws must be complied with," the judge said.
However he said he was not giving the maximum prison term because Tsuda had been a "significant source of information" in the government's investigation of the scandal.
"He did not attempt to minimize his role to evoke sympathy or curry favor," the judge said.

Tsuda's lawyer, Stanley Arkin, asked that his client be spared a prison term because of the cultural differences between Japan and the United States. He said that following orders is much more ingrained in Japanese society than in the United States. He also said that Tsuda and his family would be ostrasized by society because of a prison sentence.
Stein rejected the arguments and said that Tsuda had been "quite clear" about understanding U.S. law and its consequences.
"I had an obligation to follow U.S. law, and I and others should have done so," Tsuda told Stein. "I want to stress...how truly sorry I am for any harm I caused the United States and its people."
Tsuda said he had learned of the trading losses in a telephone call from Japan on July 25, 1995 less than three weeks after becoming general manager of the branch.

Tsuda said the deputy president of Daiwa had instructed him to assist in an internal probe of the loss and the findings were not to be disclosed until after September 30, the end of Daiwa's fiscal year.
